name: Opus-fleet dividend growth
strategy: Concentrated in 25+ year dividend aristocrats and quality dividend-grower ETFs with defensive staples/healthcare tilt, funded by strong free cash flow, harvesting 4% cash yield on the sleeve.

positions.thesis: Held flat at 40% and the flat hold is a deliberate refusal, not inertia. The obvious home for capital freed by an exit and two trims was to push the rules-based core to 47-50%, and I checked that assumption instead of acting on it: SCHD's largest holding is ABT at 4.76% (2.37% upside to consensus), its second is AMGN at 4.58% ($439.33 against a $388.48 target, 11.57% DOWNSIDE), and its third is MRK at 4.42% ($152.55 against $147.77, 3.13% downside even after the positive Moderna melanoma-vaccine Phase 3 read and a wave of target raises to $160-$179). Roughly 14% of the fund sits in three names the sell-side thinks are at or through fair value. Adding here would not diversify away from my compression problem, it would buy more of it at 0.06%. So the fund keeps every property I selected it for — 32.31% trailing 1-year total return, 2.99% yield, $109.5B AUM, a 0.69 beta and a screen that mechanically rotates toward cash-flow quality without my having to have an opinion — and it stays the largest thing I own at 49% of gross, but it absorbs none of this week's proceeds. It is at an all-time high, which I note and again do not treat as a sell signal, because this is a rebalancing basket rather than a momentum position with a price memory. The 12% stop remains portfolio-level catastrophe protection on a 100-name vehicle, not a trading stop, and there is still no take-profit: you do not take profits on the compounding core.

Trimmed from 13% to 10%. Last week I sized this at 13% on one explicit, stated property: it was the widest gap in the book at $249.46 against a $276.24 consensus, 10.74% upside when everything else offered 4.7%-8.5%. In five sessions the stock did +6.2% to $264.96 and the gap closed to 4.39% against a $276.59 target from 31 analysts. The property I paid the extra weight for no longer exists, so the extra weight comes off — that is the whole trim, and it is a valuation fact rather than a change of mind about the company. Nothing has broken in the business: forward PE is a perfectly reasonable 17.5 (the 74.9 trailing is IPR&D accounting noise, not deterioration), the FY26 revenue guide of ~$67.6B is intact, and management continues to describe the immunology franchise built around Skyrizi as the long-term growth driver, which is exactly the engine that produced the Q2 beat I waited out. A 53-year consecutive raise streak at a 2.61% yield remains a top-tier holding in a dividend-growth mandate, which is why 10% is still my largest single name and roughly a quarter of my direct equity risk. It is not larger because the Apogee acquisition dilution I flagged last week is still absorbed in the FY26 adjusted EPS guide of $13.87-$14.07, and because paying up for a name trading 4% from consensus is precisely what I am selling elsewhere. Take-profit resets to +7%, near $283.5 — above the consensus rather than at it, so it only fills if the immunology momentum beats again rather than on a drift into the analyst number. Stop tightens from 12% to 10% to protect the +6.2% already banked on the mark; there is no earnings event before the next reassessment, so 10% is ample room.

Held flat at 9%, and the specific reason for flat rather than up is the calendar: Medtronic reports September 1, ten days out and after my next reassessment, so I would be carrying an unhedged earnings binary at a size I chose for a different reason. On the merits it wants more weight. It is now the second-best name I own on the two axes my mandate scores — a 3.09% yield, the richest among healthcare aristocrats, plus 5.45% upside to a $98.44 consensus from 29 analysts — and the valuation gap that defines the thesis is intact and quantified: 15.7x forward against 25.0x trailing says the sell-side has fully modelled an earnings recovery that has not yet shown up in reported numbers. That recovery is visible in the top line already, with FY26 revenue of $36.36B up 8.43% year over year even as net income grew only 2.98%, which is the margin-lag signature of a turnaround mid-flight rather than a stalled one. The UBS upgrade to Buy with a $100 target gave me a named catalyst last week and the stock has since added 2.3% to $93.35 from my $91.27 entry, so the position is working. The pipeline keeps converting — expanded CE Mark for Affera in ventricular arrhythmias, SPR Therapeutics and Scientia Vascular closed, AI-powered surgical technology unveiled. At a 0.57 beta this remains the book's designated low-beta ballast, the role I moved it into when I retired JNJ for costing twice as much per unit of the same function. The 10% stop stays deliberately tight for a core hold precisely because of September 1; take-profit at +10% sits near $102.7, above the $98.44 consensus, which is where a genuine beat-and-raise would put it and nowhere a drift would.

Held flat at 7% and this is the hardest hold in the book, because on my own scorecard CVX now ranks first among everything I already own — a 3.47% yield plus 6.14% upside to a $217.88 consensus from 25 analysts, at 13.3x forward with a 0.49 beta. The mechanical read says add back the two points I cut last week. I am not doing it, and the reason is discipline over opportunism. I cut this leg from 9% to 7% on an explicit stated principle: I had flagged at entry that this was the one position with genuine one-headline reversal risk because the earnings were levered to a Middle East geopolitical premium, that risk became an actual headline when Chevron itself attributed the $12.1B Q2 net income to that premium and Trump publicly attacked the majors over $48B of quarterly Big Oil profits, and I wrote that the disciplined response to a flagged risk materialising is to bank part of the gain rather than re-underwrite at a worse price. The stock then rose 2.6% to $205.27 through exactly that week. Buying it back one week later and $5 higher because the market shrugged would mean my stated rule survives only until it costs me something, and a rule that only binds when it is free is not a rule. The underlying franchise continues to deliver — a condensate discovery at the 105-4X well in Angola's Block 0, Equinor taking a 17.4% stake in the offshore Namibia license — and at 7% this stays my sole energy line and my second-highest yield, earning its income-sleeve capital. The 10% stop remains for the unchanged one-headline reason; take-profit moves to +8%, around $221.7, just through the $214.71 52-week high, which a crude spike can reach and a drift cannot.

New position at 5%, funded directly out of the KO trim — this is a rotation within staples, not an increase in staples exposure, which stays at 10% of a 81% gross book. The pair speaks for itself: I am selling half of a beverage aristocrat trading at 26.8x forward for a 2.33% yield at its 52-week high with 3.95% upside, and buying a beverage-and-snacks aristocrat at 16.5x forward for a 4.13% yield sitting 16% below its $171.48 high with 8% upside to $155. On the yield-plus-upside scorecard my mandate runs on, PEP scores 12.1 against a best-in-legacy-book 9.6. The streak that qualifies it is not merely intact but freshly extended: 54 consecutive years of increases and a 4% raise just declared, with an ex-dividend date of September 4 that I collect. I am stating the bear case rather than burying it, because it is the whole reason the yield exists. Consensus is 'Hold' not 'Buy', Citi and others have cut targets in recent weeks, 2025 earnings fell 13.97% on $93.93B of revenue, North America remains weak despite price reductions, and Frito-Lay is the specific drag as American snacking behaviour shifts. That is genuine core deceleration — the same pattern that made me exit P&G — and I want to be precise about why I am buying it here and sold it there. P&G was deceleration at a full multiple with outside spending layered on top; PEP is deceleration already marked down to 16.5x with a 4.13% yield paying me to wait, which is the difference between a thesis breaking and a thesis being priced. I size it at only 5% rather than matching the old KO weight because a 'Hold' consensus with active downgrades is a knife I do not need to catch two-handed. Next earnings are October 8, well past the next reassessment, so the 12% stop is wide by design — the snacks recovery will be noisy and I do not want to be shaken out of a 4%+ yield by tape noise. Take-profit at +12%, near $160.7, sits above the $155 consensus because a real North America inflection re-rates the multiple rather than just closing the target gap.

New position at 5%, and the highest-scoring security in my entire screened universe: a 5.20% yield plus 8.96% upside to a $68.21 consensus from 24 analysts, scoring 14.2 against 9.6 for the best thing I already owned. It qualifies squarely on the mandate's defining test — 30 consecutive years of annual dividend increases, a Dividend Aristocrat, and 674 consecutive monthly common dividends, which is a longer unbroken payment record than anything else in this book. The 'funded by strong free cash flow' clause is met more literally here than anywhere: net-lease rent from 15,500+ properties across 50 states and nine countries is contractual income, not a margin forecast, and the tenant base skews to the defensive retail my mandate already tilts toward — grocery, convenience, dollar and drug stores — so this is staples exposure by revenue source even though it is a REIT by structure. The near-term evidence is good rather than merely stable: Q2 2026 revenue of $1.55B beat consensus on robust investment activity and management RAISED full-year guidance, so I am buying into an upgrade cycle, not a value trap. I collect the August 31 ex-dividend date. Two honest caveats. The headline 45.8x P/E is a REIT accounting artifact — depreciation swamps GAAP earnings and AFFO in the low-to-mid teens is the real multiple — but I note it rather than pretending it away. And the consensus rating is 'Hold', with rate sensitivity the obvious risk if the long end backs up. I accept that specific risk knowingly, because the alternative use of this capital is cash at 4%, and O pays 120bp more with 9% of price upside and a three-decade raise streak attached. Sized at 5% because rate duration is a factor I do not otherwise carry and I want it present, not dominant. The 10% stop respects that duration risk; take-profit at +10%, around $68.9, sits just through the consensus.

Trimmed again from 9% to 5%, the second consecutive cut, and the consistency is the point. Last week I took it 13% to 9% on the stated grounds that 26.4x for a 2.42% yield with single-digit upside was too much weight; the stock then added 3.9% to $91.10 and made the exact same argument louder — 27.4x trailing and 26.8x forward, the yield down to 2.33%, and just 3.95% upside to a $94.70 consensus, with the price now pressed against a $91.87 52-week high. It is the second-worst name in the book on both axes I score. If I would not buy it here, and at 3.95% upside I would not, then holding 9% of it is a decision I am making by default rather than on purpose, so I cut it to the weight I would actually initiate. I keep 5% rather than exiting entirely because unlike ABT the business is genuinely accelerating into the valuation: FY26 guidance was raised on the Q2 print, 2025 earnings rose 23.29% on 1.87% revenue growth, EPS is up 18.0% to $3.33, volume and organic revenue growth are intact, several firms pushed targets above $95 after the quarter, and the 62-year King's streak is the longest raise record among my direct equity lines. The fairlife cybersecurity incident that halted four US facilities resolved with production resumed and remains a contained subsidiary event, not a franchise issue. So this stays a real holding at a size proportionate to a 3.95% expected return, with the four points it gives up going straight across to PEP at nearly double the yield and 16% off its high. Take-profit comes down again to +5%, about $95.7, which sits just above consensus in the zone where post-Q2 target raises actually landed and is therefore a fillable order rather than a wish. Stop tightens from 9% to 8% because a name at its 52-week high on 26.8x forward has further to fall on a miss than one with a valuation cushion.

reassessment_note: Weekly desk 2026-08-22: My own framework, applied honestly, forces this. Last week I trimmed on the grounds that upside had compressed into a 4.7%-10.7% band; one week and another +6.28% NAV later that band is 2.37%-6.14%, and the weighted upside-to-consensus on the equity book is now roughly 4% against a risk-free cash rate of 4% APY. The forward equity risk premium on the specific securities I own has gone to about zero, and the correct response in an income mandate is not to hold on for sentiment but to sell what has crossed its own target and redeploy into 25+ year raisers that still pay me to take the risk. ABT is the cleanest case: at 2.37% upside and a 2.16% yield it now scores worse on both mandate axes than XOM did when I retired XOM for precisely that, and I keep ~1.9% effective exposure through SCHD as its largest holding, so the direct line is pure duplication at 37.7x earnings. ABBV loses the size premium I paid for the widest-gap-in-book property because that property is gone — 10.74% upside became 4.39% in five sessions. KO is at its 52-week high on 26.8x forward for a 2.33% yield. Critically, I checked whether SCHD was the place to park the proceeds and it is not: its top three holdings (ABT, AMGN at -11.57%, MRK at -3.13% to consensus) are as extended as my singles, so the core stays flat at 40% rather than absorbing the capital. Instead the money goes to the two aristocrats that are cheap for identifiable, priced-in reasons — PEP at 4.13% and 16% off its high, O at 5.20% with guidance just raised — and the remainder to cash, which my mandate explicitly names as a 4%-yielding sleeve and which currently out-yields four of my seven equity legs outright. I deliberately did NOT re-add to CVX even though it now ranks best in the legacy book, because last week I cut it on the stated principle that you bank gains when a flagged risk becomes an actual headline; re-buying it one week later at a higher price because the market shrugged would be opportunism overriding the rule, and the rule is worth more than two points of weight. MDT stays flat rather than upsized purely because its earnings land September 1, after my next reassessment, and I do not add into a print. Turnover is ~14% sold and 10% bought at ~2bps a side, well under a basis point of NAV — this is not churn, it is the mandate reasserting itself.
novelty: I manage no Round-2 book, so there is no overlap to police; this book is my sole entry and shares no positions with any other book I run.
research_notes:

The BTC $63k-to-$78k run and the six standing orders that fired across the field are entirely irrelevant to this book. Pulled fresh 2026-08-21 closes, yields, forward multiples, consensus targets and earnings dates on all six holdings plus four replacement candidates (PEP, MRK, AMGN, O). The single dominant finding is that the book rallied again and priced itself out of my own mandate:

THE AGGREGATE FACT: last week I wrote that every leg had compressed into a 4.7%-10.7% upside band and called that the reason to stop concentrating. One week later that band is 2.37%-6.14%. The weighted average upside-to-consensus across the equity book is now roughly 4%, against a cash rate of 4% APY. On a 12-month consensus view the equity risk premium on my own holdings has gone to approximately zero. That is the decision, not any single-name news.

I also checked whether the basket I own is any better: SCHD's #1 holding is ABT (2.37% upside) and its #2 is AMGN at $439.33 against a $388.48 consensus — 11.57% DOWNSIDE. Its #3 MRK at $152.55 against $147.77 is 3.13% downside, even after the positive Moderna melanoma-vaccine Phase 3 and target raises to $160-$179, with one shop downgrading on "unprecedented valuation." So adding to SCHD is not an escape from the compression problem; its own top sleeve is as stretched as my single names. That killed the obvious "park it in the core" answer.

REPLACEMENT CANDIDATES SCREENED:
- PEP $143.48, 4.13% yield, 18.8x trailing / 16.5x forward, 8% upside to $155, and 16% BELOW its $171.48 52-week high. 54-year raise streak just extended with a fresh 4% increase declared, ex-div Sept 4, next earnings Oct 8. The bear case is real and I am not hiding from it: consensus is "Hold" not "Buy," Citi and others have cut targets, North America snacking demand is genuinely weak and 2025 earnings fell 14%. Yield+upside = 12.1 vs. a best-in-book 9.6 (CVX).

Q2 2026 revenue $1.55B beat and FY guidance RAISED on robust investment activity. 15,500+ properties, defensive net-lease tenant mix. Yield+upside = 14.2, the best available anywhere in my universe. P/E is meaningless for a REIT; the relevant risk is rate sensitivity, and it trades mid-range ($55.86-$67.94), not extended.
- AMGN and MRK both screened out on negative consensus upside — I own both indirectly through SCHD and will not add direct lines.

Ranking my universe on the two axes my mandate actually cares about (yield + upside to consensus): O 14.2, PEP 12.1, CVX 9.6, MDT 8.5, ABBV 7.0, KO 6.3, ABT 4.5. ABT now scores worse on both axes than XOM did (2.57% yield / 5.28% upside) when I retired XOM last week for exactly that reason.
